abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Early prediction of response to neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) is crucial for optimizing breast cancer treatment strategies. Here, we present a novel breast self-supervised temporal learning framework (BSTNet) for predicting the pathological complete response (pCR) using longitudinal MRI. Through self-supervised pre-training, BSTNet aims to achieve model generalization across multi-timepoint and dual-timepoint scenarios while capturing dynamic tumor changes during NAT. In a multicenter cohort of 1339 patients, BSTNet demonstrated robust performance: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.882 in internal validation (from Center 1), and 0.857 and 0.854 in external validation (Centers 2 and 3, respectively). In all three validation cohorts, subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent performance across molecular subtypes, with AUCs ranging from 0.827 to 0.886 for hormone receptor status and 0.818–0.895 for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 status. The model maintained a stable performance across varying interim MRI timings in the external validation cohorts, with AUCs of 0.841–0.893 in Center 2 and 0.792–0.970 in Center 3. Notably, BSTNet effectively identified patients with non-pCR (specificity: 86.4%, 74.5%, and 85.1% for internal validation, Center 2, and Center 3, respectively). In conclusion, BSTNet provides a robust and generalizable deep learning framework for early pCR prediction. Its ability to effectively interpret variable longitudinal MRI data offers a powerful and practical tool to guide adaptive treatment planning in diverse clinical settings.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Breast cancer is the most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women1. Neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) has emerged as a critical part of current systemic treatment of breast cancer. Achieving pathological complete response (pCR) to NAT allows for surgical de-escalation, making patients eligible for breast-conserving surgery instead of mastectomy2,3. More importantly, pCR serves as a validated surrogate endpoint that strongly predicts improved long-term survival4–6. However, despite these significant clinical benefits, only about 19–30% of patients achieve pCR4,7–9. Therefore, early prediction of pCR is crucial, as neoadjuvant trials have demonstrated improved pCR rates and patient outcomes with timely treatment adjustments10,11. This underscores the critical need for reliable methods to predict pCR early during NAT, facilitating personalized treatment adaptation in breast cancer management.

Previous studies have explored using blood or tissue biopsy biomarkers to predict pCR12,13. These approaches have not gained widespread clinical adoption owing to their invasive nature, high costs, and limited validation in large-scale populations. As a non-invasive modality, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) provides comprehensive tumor response assessment and shows greater feasibility for clinical application14. Despite these advantages, traditional MRI analysis methods have not achieved sufficient accuracy for reliable pCR prediction15.

Deep learning approaches have shown promise in analyzing medical images for therapeutic evaluation16,17. These studies focused on imaging features from a single time point analysis, overlooking the biological and morphological changes that occur during treatment. Longitudinal imaging data may provide valuable information for response prediction by characterizing these temporal changes. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled the analysis of longitudinal imaging data, showing promise in predicting the response to NAT with performance surpassing single-time-point analyses18–20. However, these studies relied on medical images from two fixed time points, typically analyzing pre-treatment and post-treatment scans through simple feature concatenation18,20. Such approaches may not effectively capture the complex temporal evolution of tumor characteristics. Moreover, the varying intervals between scans in clinical practice pose additional challenges for conventional analytical methods, highlighting the need for more flexible and robust approaches to temporal modeling.

In this study, we developed a novel self-supervised temporal learning framework to analyze longitudinal breast cancer MRI scans. Our approach leverages self-supervised pre-training to learn temporal features from variable-length imaging sequences, enabling the capture of complex dynamic changes during treatment. The framework demonstrated robust performance across different molecular subtypes and varying scan intervals, addressing common clinical challenges in which imaging protocols and timing often differ between institutions. This adaptability to different scanning schedules renders it suitable for real-world clinical applications.

sec.title: Clinicopathologic characteristics
sec.p: In this study, 1339 consecutive patients with 3928 MRI scans were included in the final analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1, Table 1). pCR was achieved in 180 (34.0%) of 529 patients in the training cohort (mean age, 48.6 ± 10.2 years), 45 (33.8%) of 133 patients in the internal validation cohort (mean age, 48.5 ± 10.6 years), 134 (35.2%) of 381 patients in Center 2 (mean age, 49.1 ± 9.8 years), and 101 (34.1%) of 296 patients in Center 3 (mean age, 48.0 ± 10.8 years). The hormone receptor (HR) status and molecular subtypes differed significantly between the pCR and non-pCR groups across all cohorts (P < 0.05). Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive status was associated with increased pCR rates in both the internal and external validation cohorts (P < 0.05). A high Ki-67 status ( ≥ 30%) was significantly associated with higher pCR rates in both external validation cohorts (P < 0.05). Age across all cohorts, and T stage, N stage, and histological type in the external validation cohorts showed no significant differences between the pCR and non-pCR groups (all P > 0.05). Detailed clinicopathological characteristics are presented in Table 1.

sec.p: Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify clinical predictors of pCR (Supplementary Table 1). The resulting clinical model served as a baseline for comparison with other prediction approaches.

sec.title: Model performance for response prediction
sec.p: Our proposed BSTNet demonstrated superior discriminatory performance for predicting NAT response across all validation cohorts, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.882 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.816–0.948] in internal validation, 0.857 [95% CI: 0.819–0.895] in Center 2, and 0.854 [95% CI: 0.802–0.906] in Center 3 (Fig. 1A, C, E). For a comprehensive evaluation, we compared BSTNet with four benchmark methods: (1) a multi-temporal model without self-supervised learning (No-SSL), (2) a radiomics model, (3) a clinical model, and (4) a single-scan deep learning model. Statistical analysis revealed that BSTNet significantly outperformed all the other models in the external validation cohort (Fig. 1D, F). In internal validation, BSTNet showed significant improvement over all approaches except the radiomics model, where the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. 1B). The No-SSL model ranked second in performance, with AUCs of 0.813 [95% CI: 0.739–0.887] in internal validation, 0.783 [95% CI: 0.736–0.830] in Center 2, and 0.759 [95% CI: 0.694–0.823] in Center 3. Conventional approaches demonstrate varying cross-center stability. The radiomics model performed comparably to BSTNet in internal validation (AUC: 0.827 [95% CI: 0.751–0.903]) but showed substantial performance decline in external validation cohorts (AUC: 0.602 [95% CI: 0.558–0.646] in Center 2; 0.710 [95% CI: 0.646–0.774] in Center 3). The clinical model maintained consistent but moderate performance across all cohorts (AUCs: 0.738, 0.705, and 0.733 for internal validation, Center 2, and Center 3, respectively). The single-scan deep learning approach exhibited moderate discriminatory ability in internal validation (AUC: 0.753) but significant performance deterioration in external validation (AUCs: 0.643 and 0.613 for Centers 2 and 3, respectively).

sec.p: The radar plots demonstrated the comprehensive performance of different models across six metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, PPV, and NPV) in the three cohorts (Fig. 2A–C). BSTNet consistently showed a balanced and superior performance across all metrics. The comprehensive performance metrics are detailed in Table 2 and Supplementary Tables 2–5. Decision curve analysis revealed that BSTNet had a slightly lower net benefit than the radiomic model in internal validation. However, BSTNet demonstrated superior performance in both external validation cohorts across threshold probabilities of 0.3–0.7 (Fig. 2D–F). Notably, BSTNet effectively identified patients with non-pCR across all cohorts, achieving specificities of 86.4% (76/88) in internal validation, 74.5% (184/247) in Center 2, and 85.1% (166/195) in Center 3 (Fig. 3A–C). The calibration curve of BSTNet demonstrated good consistency between the predicted and actual pCR in all cohorts (Fig. 3D).

sec.title: Subgroup analysis of the BSTNet
sec.p: BSTNet demonstrated consistent performance across different molecular subtypes in all validation cohorts (Supplementary Figs. 2–4). For HR status, no statistically significant differences were observed between the HR- and HR+ subtypes, with AUCs ranging from 0.827 to 0.886 across all cohorts (Supplementary Table 6). Similarly, for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status, the model showed comparable performance between HER2- and HER2+ tumors without statistically significant differences, with AUCs ranging from 0.818 to 0.895 across all cohorts (Supplementary Table 6).

We also performed subgroup analyses based on the timing of the interim MRI scans within the external validation cohorts, as detailed in Supplementary Fig. 5. In Center 2, BSTNet demonstrated robust and stable performance regardless of when the scan was acquired, with consistently high AUCs ranging from 0.841 to 0.893 across courses 1–4 (Supplementary Fig. 6, Supplementary Table 7). In contrast, the model’s performance in Center 3 varied, peaking in course 4 (AUC = 0.970), substantially outperforming its accuracy in course 2 (AUC = 0.863) and course 3 (AUC = 0.792) (Supplementary Fig. 7, Supplementary Table 8).

sec.title: Model interpretation
sec.p: Activation mapping was employed to visualize the regions within the MRI that significantly contributed to model predictions, where the intensity magnitude indicates the importance of each pixel. This visualization approach helps clinicians understand the intratumoral and peritumoral regions that influence the BSTNet predictions. As shown in Fig. 4, a distinct temporal evolution of activation patterns was observed between pCR and non-pCR cases from the pre-treatment to early-treatment phases. In non-pCR patients (Fig. 4A, B), post-treatment activation heatmaps demonstrated a notable concentration in the peripheral regions of the tumor. In contrast, pCR cases (Fig. 4C, D) exhibited more centralized activation patterns, with the highest intensities concentrated within the core tumor region. This differential spatial distribution of activation features suggests that the deep learning model may capture distinct radiological characteristics associated with the treatment response patterns.

sec.p: In addition, we selected four representative patients whose outcomes were misclassified by the BSTNet model to further investigate the model’s decision-making process. In non-pCR cases erroneously predicted as pCR (Supplementary Fig. 8A, B), significant central tumor necrosis was common on pre-treatment MRI. The model’s initial attention focused on peripheral viable tumor regions; subsequently, activation shifted centrally after treatment, appearing as a ‘centralized activation pattern’. Conversely, for patients who achieved pCR but were incorrectly predicted as non-pCR by BSTNet (Supplementary Fig. 8C, D), the activation heatmaps revealed that the model’s attention was not exclusively confined to the lesion. Instead, activation often extends beyond the lesion to include non-lesional areas such as the vasculature or adjacent normal tissues.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we developed a novel self-supervised temporal deep learning framework to predict tumor response in patients with breast cancer undergoing neoadjuvant therapy. Our BSTNet model demonstrated robust and consistent performance in predicting pCR, achieving AUCs of 0.882, 0.857, and 0.854 in internal validation, Center 2, and Center 3, respectively. Importantly, BSTNet’s performance remained stable across the various molecular subtypes and scanning intervals. Notably, BSTNet exhibited robust specificity in identifying non-pCR patients (86.4%, 74.5%, and 85.1% in the respective cohorts). This capability could enable clinicians to make timely adjustments to treatment strategies for patients who are unlikely to achieve pCR and reduce unnecessary treatment-related toxicities.

Single time-point imaging models have demonstrated promising results for pCR prediction17,21,22. However, this approach may not be optimal, as breast tumors undergo substantial biological and morphological changes during NAT15,23, including alterations in tumor size, vascularity, and cellular density, which single time-point imaging cannot capture. Longitudinal DCE-MRI scans provide an opportunity to monitor these dynamic changes24,25, making temporal integration crucial for accurate prediction. To capture these treatment-induced changes effectively, we developed BSTNet by leveraging a self-supervised temporal learning framework. As demonstrated in our results, BSTNet achieved substantially superior performance compared to the single scan model (AUCs: 0.882 vs 0.753 in internal validation, 0.857 vs 0.643 in Center 2, and 0.854 vs 0.613 in Center 3).

Current approaches to longitudinal imaging analysis often focus on limited time points, such as pre-treatment and pre-surgery scans18,26,27. Even methods incorporating multiple time points typically rely on simplistic feature concatenation28, which may inadequately capture the complex temporal dependencies inherent in tumor response patterns. Furthermore, these approaches usually require a matched number of sequences across all time points29, leading to the potential exclusion of valuable cases with missing data at specific intervals. Our framework introduced an innovative temporal learning strategy to address these limitations. This approach combines self-supervised pre-training with transfer learning while integrating self-attention mechanisms and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. This design effectively handles irregular sampling patterns and missing time points, capturing temporal dependencies without requiring paired data across all the scans. To validate the advantages of our approach, we compared it with conventional methods. A radiomic model using delta features between pre-treatment and the final time point demonstrated limited performance (AUCs: 0.827, 0.602, and 0.710 in the respective cohorts), indicating that simple feature differences are insufficient to fully characterize the dynamic response patterns. Subsequently, we compared BSTNet with a temporal deep learning model without self-supervised learning (No-SSL). Although the No-SSL model showed improvement over single-scan, radiomics, and clinical approaches, BSTNet consistently achieved superior results across all cohorts (AUCs: 0.882 vs 0.813, 0.857 vs 0.783, and 0.854 vs 0.759). This improvement demonstrates the effectiveness of our self-supervised temporal learning strategy in capturing complex treatment response patterns, particularly when compared with conventional feature engineering or standard temporal modeling approaches. The consistent performance advantage of BSTNet across different validation cohorts underscores how self-supervised learning enhances the robustness and generalizability of the model by capturing universal patterns of treatment response.

Previous deep-learning approaches20,25,28,30 were limited by small datasets and limited longitudinal scans. Our self-supervised learning approach leveraged the temporal permutation of longitudinal scans, effectively augmenting the training data to 2648 samples derived from 662 patients. This pre-training strategy enables the model to learn intrinsic temporal relationships without requiring additional manual annotations. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated by the model’s robust performance across different centers and scanning protocols, suggesting its ability to generalize well and capture fundamental patterns of tumor response dynamics during the self-supervised phase.

Beyond its robust technical performance, BSTNet demonstrates significant potential for clinical decision support in personalizing NAT for breast cancer. Its promising specificity in identifying non-pCR patients (e.g., 86.4% in internal validation, 74.5% in Center 2, and 85.1% in Center 3) is crucial for early treatment adaptation. This capability could allow clinicians to promptly consider alternative strategies for predicted non-responders, potentially minimizing ineffective treatment and associated toxicities. More comprehensively, our decision curve analysis confirmed the clinical utility of BSTNet. While the radiomics model showed strong performance on the internal validation set, exhibiting a net benefit comparable to or exceeding that of BSTNet, a key strength of BSTNet emerged in its consistent and superior net benefit across external validation cohorts when compared to other models. Across all cohorts, BSTNet surpassed the net benefit of treating all or no patients over a wide range of clinically relevant threshold probabilities. This indicates that incorporating BSTNet predictions could lead to improved decision-making by more accurately stratifying patients for escalation or de-escalation of therapy. The DCA results thereby underscore BSTNet’s potential to enhance net clinical outcomes, even accounting for varied performance nuances across different datasets (such as the specificity in Center 2 or the internal DCA results), provided that appropriate decision thresholds are utilized.

To enhance model interpretability, we utilized gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualization to identify the regions most influential in the model predictions. These activation patterns may correlate with previously reported tumor shrinkage patterns in breast cancer imaging studies. Centralized activation in pCR cases might be associated with the concentric shrinkage pattern reported in several MRI studies31,32, characterized by tumor reduction to small foci. Conversely, the peripheral activation patterns observed in non-pCR cases corresponded to the non-concentric shrinkage patterns documented in these studies31,32. The significance of such activation patterns in treatment response evaluation is also supported by ultrasound imaging studies33, suggesting that these visualization patterns could serve as quantitative imaging biomarkers for monitoring treatment response.

Our study has several limitations. First, although our model demonstrated robust performance across different scanning intervals, the optimal timing for early response assessment requires further investigation in prospective studies. Second, although our decision curve analysis demonstrated the clinical utility of BSTNet at various threshold probabilities, a more comprehensive health evaluation is needed. Such an analysis should include long-term impact on healthcare resource utilization and patient outcomes. Finally, we analyzed only the peak enhancement phase of DCE-MRI, and future studies could explore the potential value of other contrast phases or MRI sequences for response prediction.

In conclusion, we developed a novel self-supervised temporal deep learning framework for the early prediction of pCR in patients with breast cancer receiving NAT. This model demonstrated robust performance across multiple independent cohorts and different molecular subtypes, with reliable identification of non-pCR patients. The framework’s ability to adapt to varying imaging intervals and protocols suggests its potential for clinical implementation. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate its clinical utility in guiding personalized treatment decisions.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital (No. KY2024-840-01) and Yunnan Cancer Hospital (No. KYLX2024-262). The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the use of public datasets and the retrospective nature of the study. This study used the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) guidelines34.

sec.title: Datasets and study design
sec.p: The overall design of this study is illustrated in Fig. 5. This study included three independent cohorts of breast cancer patients who underwent NAT followed by surgery. The training cohort was derived from the I-SPY2 trial (Center 1, 2010–2016), with patients randomly assigned to the training and internal validation cohorts at an 8:2 ratio. Two external validation cohorts were obtained from Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital (Center 2; March 2015–September 2022) and Yunnan Cancer Hospital (Center 3; April 2020–November 2021). The inclusion criteria for all cohorts were: (a) pathologically confirmed invasive breast cancer, (b)surgery performed after the completion of NAT, (c) availability of pre-treatment MRI scans as well as any MRI scans taken after 1 to 4 cycles of treatment (Center 1 required three-four MRI exams before surgery), and (d) postoperative pathologic evaluation of treatment response to NAT. Exclusion criteria included: (a) inadequate quality MRI, (b) incomplete or non-standard NAT treatment or surgery, and (c) patients who had other concurrent malignancies or were receiving another oncologic treatment.

sec.title: Clinicopathologic data and endpoint definition
sec.p: Clinicopathological data included age at diagnosis, menopausal status, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, NAT regimen, histological type, HR status, HER2 status, and Ki-67 status. The pathologic information included histologic tumor grade, Ki67 proliferation index, hormone receptor (HR) status, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status of core needle biopsy or surgical resection. HR was defined as positive if tumor cells exhibited ≥1% of nuclear staining of estrogen receptor or progesterone receptor35. HER2-positive was defined as immunohistochemistry (IHC) 3+ or IHC 2+ and amplified by fluorescence in-situ hybridization36. Ki-67 expression was evaluated as either low or high, with <30% considered low expression and ≥30% considered high expression37. We collected as many clinicopathologic data as possible for I-SPY212,17. Unavailable data were treated as missing values and excluded from analyses. pCR was defined as the complete absence of invasive tumor cells in both the breast and axillary lymph nodes (ypT0/N0 or ypTis/N0)38.

sec.title: MRI acquisition and image preprocessing
sec.p: Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) were performed using 1.5-T or 3.0-T scanners with dedicated bilateral breast coils across three centers. All acquisitions utilized fat-suppressed T1-weighted gradient-echo sequences. Gadolinium-based contrast agents were administered intravenously at 0.2 mL/kg (2 mL/s injection rate) followed by a 20-mL saline flush. The I-SPY2 protocol (Center 1) acquired DCE-MRI at least 8 min post-injection, while Centers 2 and 3 acquired five post-contrast phases at 60-s intervals. Detailed acquisition parameters are summarized in Supplementary Table 9. The post-contrast phase demonstrating peak tumor enhancement was utilized for analysis.

Tumor segmentation employed a semi-automatic approach. Initial segmentations were generated using an nnU-Net model39, then independently reviewed and manually adjusted by two radiologists (X.H. and Z.Y.X., both with 6 years of breast imaging experience) blinded to clinicopathological information using ITK-SNAP (version 3.8.0). Inter-observer agreement for the refined segmentations was assessed in 268 randomly selected patients (20% of cohort) using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for tumor volume and the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) for spatial overlap, demonstrating excellent reproducibility (ICC = 0.952, mean DSC = 0.944). All VOIs were subsequently examined by a senior radiologist (W.Z., 7 years of experience), with final consensus achieved through discussion among all three radiologists for any disagreements.

Image preprocessing comprised three sequential steps. First, images were resampled to cohort-specific median spatial resolution using cubic spline interpolation for in-plane (X-Y) and linear interpolation for through-plane (Z-axis) resampling. Second, tumor-centered 3D volumes of interest (VOIs) were extracted and resampled to standardized dimensions of 64 × 128 × 128 voxels using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Third, z-score intensity normalization was applied using parameters (μ = 244.46, σ = 383.74) derived by calculating statistics across all foreground voxels identified by thresholding within the training dataset, and consistently applied to all validation cohorts.

sec.title: Self-supervised temporal deep learning
sec.p: To learn robust and generalizable feature representations that can effectively capture treatment response patterns in breast MRI40, we developed a novel breast self-supervised temporal learning framework (BSTNet). This framework integrates information from I-SPY2 longitudinal DCE-MRI scans acquired at multiple timepoints17: pre-treatment (T0), after 1 cycle of NAT (T1), after 4 cycles of NAT (T2), and pre-surgery (T3). The temporal distribution of available scans is shown in Supplementary Fig. 9. For self-supervised learning, we utilized 662 patients with complete three or four-timepoint sequences. Through controlled temporal permutation, we generated an augmented dataset of 2648 samples, where each patient contributed one positive sample (original sequence: T0 → T1 → T2 → T3) and three negative samples (randomly permuted sequences). This approach enables the model to learn temporal relationships without additional manual labeling. For computational efficiency, the ROI extraction included a 3 mm margin extension around tumor volumes, and input dimensions were standardized to (64, 128, 128) voxels per timepoint. To handle potential missing timepoints in clinical practice, the framework incorporates normalized feature extraction and cross-timepoint attention mechanisms.

sec.title: BSTNet pipeline architecture and model development
sec.p: The proposed BSTNet consists of three main components (Fig. 6): a 3D ResNet18 CNN backbone for spatial feature extraction and a temporal processing pipeline integrating Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and LSTM modules41–43. The CNN backbone, truncated at the global average pooling layer, independently processes each temporal scan to generate 256-dimensional feature representations. These features are processed through an 8-head attention mechanism and an LSTM network, maintaining consistent dimensionality throughout the pipeline. sec.p: Model training followed a two-stage protocol implemented in PyTorch: initial self-supervised learning with temporal permutation, followed by supervised fine-tuning for pCR prediction. Five-fold cross-validation was employed with the following configuration: batch size of 16, 500 epochs, Adam optimizer (learning rate: 1 × 10⁻³, weight decay: 5 × 10⁻⁴), and a linear learning rate scheduler. Data augmentation was implemented using the MONAI framework, incorporating random affine transformations (rotation: ±15°, scale: ±10%, translation: ±5 voxels), contrast adjustment (gamma: 0.5–2.0), and 3D rotations ( ± 15° per axis). During supervised fine-tuning, encoder layers were frozen while temporal processing components and classification layers were updated using weighted cross-entropy loss with dynamically computed class weights. For external validation with varying scanning intervals, zero-padding was employed to maintain consistent input structure.

sec.title: Comparative models
sec.p: For a comprehensive performance evaluation, we established four comparative models: (1) a clinical model, (2) a radiomics model, (3) a single-scan deep learning model, and (4) No-SSL. The clinical model was constructed using significant predictors from multivariable analysis common to all cohorts (Supplementary Table 1). HR and HER2 status were retained based on their established biological relevance to treatment response, despite HR status not reaching statistical significance in Center 3. Molecular subtype was excluded due to collinearity with HR and HER2 status.

The radiomics model utilized delta features computed as the difference between pre-treatment and last-timepoint DCE-MRI. Features were extracted using PyRadiomics (version 3.0.1) with bin width of 25, B-spline interpolation, and isotropic voxel resampling (1 × 1× 1 mm³). Three feature types were extracted: (1) original delta features (first-order statistics, shape, and texture), (2) LoG-filtered delta features (sigma: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), and (3) wavelet-transformed delta features. Feature selection combined Mann–Whitney U test (α = 0.05), LASSO regression (α = 0.01), and Pearson correlation analysis (threshold = 0.3), retaining the top 25 most discriminative features.

The single-scan deep learning model employed an identical 3D ResNet18 architecture as BSTNet but processed only pre-surgery (T3) or after 1 ~ 4 cycle MRI scans, maintaining consistent hyperparameters and data augmentation strategies for fair comparison.
The No-SSL model replicated BSTNet’s complete architecture but excluded the self-supervised learning phase, training directly on the pCR prediction task with identical protocols.

sec.title: Evaluation of model performance
sec.p: The model performance was evaluated using multiple metrics. The primary metric was the AUC with 95% CI. Additional performance metrics included accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value. The calibration of all models was evaluated in the training and validation groups through calibration curves. The clinical utility of the models was assessed using decision curve analysis. To interpret the model’s decision-making process, we employed Grad-CAM to visualize the regions that contributed most significantly to the pCR prediction.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) based on the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, and categorical variables as frequencies (percentages). Between-group comparisons were performed using Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with pCR. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariable analysis were included in the subsequent multivariable analysis.

Model performance was evaluated using AUC with 95% CIs, calculated through 1000 bootstrap resamples. The optimal cutoff value was determined using the Youden index. Inter-model comparisons were conducted using DeLong’s test44. Given the null hypothesis of an AUC of 0.50, alternate hypothesis of an AUC of 0.80, pCR proportion of 30%, and statistical power of 90%, the minimum required sample size in the external test set was 44 participants. Decision curve analysis calculates the net benefit across different threshold probabilities. Calibration curves were fitted and evaluated using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test. All statistical tests were two-sided, with significance set at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.2) and Python (version 3.12).
